The Bi-LSTM Utterance Encoder encodes the user utterance at each dialogue turn into a continuous vector representation. It does this by mapping the words of the user utterance to an embedding space and then processing them through a bidirectional LSTM. The final user utterance vector is formed by concatenating the last forward and backward LSTM states. This encoded user utterance vector, together with the encoding of the previous system action, serves as input to the dialogue-level LSTM, which maintains the dialogue state. (Page 3)

The system generates a response by first encoding the user utterance into a continuous vector using a bidirectional LSTM. This encoding, along with the encoding of the previous system action, is input to a dialogue-level LSTM that maintains a continuous dialogue state representation. Based on this state, the model predicts probability distributions over candidate values for each tracked goal slot. These outputs are used to formulate a query command to a knowledge base (KB) to retrieve information. The system then produces a dialogue action conditioned on the dialogue state, the estimated user goal, and the query results. Finally, this dialogue action, together with the user goal tracking results and the query results, is used by a natural language generator (NLG) to produce the final natural language system response (Page 3).

The inputs to the Translation Ranking model are the source text, the MT hypothesis, and the reference translation. These three inputs are encoded by a cross-lingual encoder to map them into a shared feature space. (Page 2)

The Translation Ranking model processes its inputs by encoding the source, MT hypothesis, and reference translation using a pretrained cross-lingual encoder (XLM-RoBERTa base). It produces embeddings for each token and each layer, then pools information from important encoder layers into a single embedding per token using a layer-wise attention mechanism. The model is trained to minimize the distance between a "better" hypothesis and both its corresponding reference and original source, mapping all three inputs into a shared feature space. Both the encoder and pooling layer are used in this process (Page 2).

The purpose of the triplet margin loss in the Translation Ranking model is to minimize the distance between a "better" hypothesis and both its corresponding reference and its original source, effectively training the model to rank better translations closer to the reference and source in the embedding space (Page 2).
